# Day 2: Programming Prerequisites

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to write and use your own
Python functions and classes, explain what a tensor is and how it
generalizes the vectors and matrices from Day 1, create and manipulate
tensors (indexing, slicing, reshaping), and explain what automatic
differentiation computes and why it matters for everything from Day 7
onward.

## Why classes, and why now

The previous run of this course covered Python syntax but never object-
oriented programming — a gap several students flagged directly ("we were
never taught classes") when the material later assumed familiarity with
it. This session treats functions and classes as new material, not
review.

A **function** bundles a sequence of steps under a name so it can be
reused without repeating the steps:

```python
def gc_content(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.upper()
    gc = sum(1 for base in sequence if base in "GC")
    return gc / len(sequence)

gc_content("ATGCGATACG")  # 0.5
```

A **class** goes one step further, bundling *data* and the *functions
that operate on that data* together into a single object. Where a
function takes data and returns a result, a class lets you create many
independent objects that each carry their own data and know how to
compute things about themselves:

```python
class DnaSequence:
    def __init__(self, name, bases):
        self.name = name
        self.bases = bases.upper()

    def gc_content(self):
        gc = sum(1 for base in self.bases if base in "GC")
        return gc / len(self.bases)

seq = DnaSequence("my_gene", "ATGCGATACG")
seq.gc_content()  # 0.5, but now seq also remembers its own name and bases
```

`__init__` is a special method Python calls automatically when a new
object is created — it's where you set up whatever data that object
should carry (here, `name` and `bases`). Every other method takes `self`
as its first argument, which just refers to "the particular object this
method was called on." This pattern — an object that owns its data and
the operations on that data — is exactly what you'll see again in Day 9,
where a neural network is itself a class that owns its weights and knows
how to compute a prediction from them.

### Further reading

- Python's own tutorial, [Classes](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html) — inheritance, class vs. instance variables, and more than this course needs
- *A Byte of Python*, [Object Oriented Programming](https://python.swaroopch.com/oop.html) — the same ground as above, at the same level

## Tensors: the data structure underneath everything from here on

Day 1 worked with vectors (a list of numbers) and matrices (a grid of
numbers). A **tensor** is the general version of both: a container for
numbers with any number of dimensions — a single number (a 0-dimensional
tensor), a vector (1-dimensional), a matrix (2-dimensional), or higher
still (a stack of matrices, and so on). Every deep-learning framework,
including PyTorch, represents all of its data — inputs, weights,
gradients — as tensors, precisely so that the same operations (add,
multiply, reshape, ...) work regardless of how many dimensions the data
happens to have.

The notebook below builds tensors out of a small DNA-encoded toy
dataset, then works through indexing, slicing, and reshaping — the same
operations you already used on Day 1's vectors and matrices, just
generalized.

## Automatic differentiation

Day 1 introduced the gradient and worked it out by hand using the chain
rule. Doing that by hand does not scale to a function with thousands or
millions of variables — which is exactly what a neural network's weights
are. **Automatic differentiation** (autograd) is the mechanism that
makes this practical: PyTorch tracks every operation performed on a
tensor, and when you ask for the gradient of some final result, it
replays those operations backward, applying the chain rule automatically
at every step. You never write a derivative by hand again after this
point in the course — you only ever call `.backward()`.

### Further reading

- PyTorch, [A Gentle Introduction to torch.autograd](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/blitz/autograd_tutorial.html) — more detail on how the computation graph is built and freed
- NumPy, [quickstart](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/quickstart.html) — the standard reference for the array operations tensors generalize

## The scientific Python stack

Beyond PyTorch, a handful of libraries recur throughout the rest of this
course, and are worth a first look now rather than being introduced
piecemeal later.

**Biopython** is what you'd actually reach for instead of writing your
own `DnaSequence` class — it already implements sequence objects (with
translation, reverse complementation, and much more), file parsing, and
database access, all used throughout real bioinformatics pipelines. Day
3's database work builds directly on it.

**NumPy** is the array library underneath almost everything else here,
including PyTorch tensors — you've effectively been using NumPy-style
thinking since the tensor section above. **pandas** builds a labeled,
tabular data structure (the `DataFrame`) on top of NumPy arrays: the
natural format for a table of many sequences and their properties, rather
than one sequence at a time.

**Matplotlib** is the base plotting library; **seaborn** builds a
higher-level, statistics-oriented interface on top of it that plugs
directly into pandas DataFrames — both are used for essentially every
figure in this book's later notebooks.

**SciPy** extends NumPy with ready-made scientific routines — statistical
tests, optimization, and more — sparing you from re-implementing standard
methods by hand.

**scikit-learn** provides ready-made, well-tested implementations of
standard machine-learning models. Day 7 deliberately builds a linear
model "by hand" with raw tensors and gradient descent, precisely so you
see every step of the mechanics — but for a plain linear regression, in
practice you would normally just call scikit-learn's implementation
directly, as the notebook below demonstrates.

### Further reading

- pandas, [10 minutes to pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/10min.html)
- scikit-learn, [Linear Models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html) user guide
- Biopython, [Tutorial and Cookbook](https://biopython.org/docs/latest/Tutorial/index.html)

Each is that library's own standard starting point for going beyond
what's shown here.

## The notebook

`notebooks/day02-tensors-and-a-first-class.ipynb` reuses this course's
own existing introductory PyTorch material almost unchanged — tensor
creation, dtypes, indexing/slicing/reshaping, and a first autograd
example, all built around a small DNA-encoded toy dataset — then adds
several new sections: a `DnaSequence` class exercise applying today's OOP
material to a real biological object, Biopython's equivalent of that same
class, a synthetic table of "genes" used to demonstrate NumPy, pandas,
Matplotlib, seaborn, SciPy, and a scikit-learn linear regression that
recovers the synthetic data's known ground-truth relationship, and
finally a recomputation of Day 1's own worked examples (a dot product and
a gradient) in code, confirming the by-hand answers match. Open it in
[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day02-tensors-and-a-first-class.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.
